requested_remedy: claims the return of the deposit and damages on the ground that certain requisitions had not been answered sufficiently or satisfactorily

facts.F1: An Agreement for Sale and Purchase dated 19 March 1997 was made between Wong Kit Chun as Vendor and Max Crown International Limited as Purchaser.
facts.F2: The property in question is Ground Floor, Lot No.2798 in Demarcation District No.130, Tuen Mun, New Territories, Hong Kong.
facts.F3: The Property is part of a small house held under New Grant No.2878 dated 23 November 1989.
facts.F4: Special Condition 5(a) and Special Condition 26 of the New Grant were subjects of requisition.
facts.F5: Special Condition 5(a) requires the allocation of one undivided 1/3rd share each to the Ground Floor, the First Floor and the Second Floor of the building on the lot.
facts.F6: The Buildings Ordinance (Application to the New Territories) Ordinance 1987 came into force on 16 October 1987 and is now Cap.121 of the Laws of Hong Kong.
facts.F7: The Title Deeds were supplied to the plaintiff's solicitors on 22 April 1997.
facts.F8: On 1 May 1997, the requisitions were raised, including the request for Certificate(s) of Exemption for building works, site formation works and drainage works pursuant to Special Condition 26(a).
facts.F9: The vendor's solicitors answered the requisitions on 7 May 1997 but the answers did not satisfy the plaintiff's solicitors.
facts.F10: Correspondences continued between the solicitors of both parties until 20 May 1997 when the defendant's solicitors informed that they were unable to obtain the documents requested without any Memorial numbers.
facts.F11: On the same day, the plaintiff's solicitors rescinded the sale and asked for the return of the deposit.
facts.F12: A letter from the District Lands Officer dated 8 December 1997 stated that no Certificate of Exemption was ever issued but the government would not take enforcement action pursuant to Special Condition (26)(a).
facts.F13: The information in the letter was not disclosed prior to 20 May 1997.
facts.F14: The defendant's solicitors gave answers on 20 May 1997 regarding Special Condition 5(a) which the court found to be sufficient and satisfactory.
facts.F15: The Certificate of Compliance does not clearly show that no Certificate of Exemption was ever issued and does not explain that any irregularity had been waived.
facts.F16: The plaintiff claimed damages, including expenses paid for rectification of electricity sockets, estate agent fee, and conveyancing expenses, which totaled HK$61,813.

reference_issues: Whether the requisition relating to the Certificate of Exemption has been sufficiently or satisfactorily answered by the defendant.
Whether the Certificate of Exemption is necessary to prove title where Cap.121 applies.

claim: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was fifty-seven years of age and worked as a waitress in a small restaurant at the time of the accident.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was detained in hospital for some nine months after the accident.
facts.F3: The plaintiff spent three months with one or both legs in traction and most of the remainder with the right leg in plaster.
facts.F4: The plaintiff received treatment and instruction in physiotherapy in the last three weeks of her hospital stay.
facts.F5: A medical report dated July 1976 indicated that the first three items of injury mentioned above have left no permanent disability.
facts.F6: The medical report also showed that there was considerable restriction in the movements of the right arm and both legs; shortening of both legs, and to different degrees; wastage of various muscles; several small scars, one of which had been remedied to some extent by a skin graft; and a substantial loss of grip strength in the right arm.
facts.F7: The plaintiff walked with a shuffling gait, could do so only slowly and for about one hour at a time and had difficulty in climbing steps.
facts.F8: The plaintiff was unfit for any form of work which involved standing or walking and was unable to lift heavy weights.
facts.F9: The doctor assessed her impairment as 15 per cent of the whole woman.
facts.F10: The plaintiff started work again for her previous employer on the 1st January that year, doing much lighter work at the reduced salary of $400 per month.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's husband spent $5,000 on providing extra nourishment to her during her recovery, but this was not recoverable as the plaintiff did not incur the expense herself.
facts.F12: The assessment of general damages was based on the plaintiff's pain and suffering, loss of amenities, and loss of future earnings.
facts.F13: The special damages were based on the plaintiff's loss of past earnings, travelling expenses, and other expenses directly related to her recovery from the injury, but not including expenses incurred by her husband.

claim: The plaintiff claims D1 failed to timely refer P to a proper specialist (such as a paediatric surgeon) despite persistent abdominal distension on 15 and 17 March 2014, resulting in P suffering permanent injuries.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims D1 failed to timely refer P to a proper specialist (such as a paediatric surgeon) despite persistent abdominal distension on 15 and 17 March 2014, resulting in P suffering permanent injuries.
parties: Plaintiff: SUN MING LOK, a minor suing by his mother and next friend, HUI MAN CHONG
Defendant: CHOY WING HO and ST TERESA’S HOSPITAL

facts.F1: D1 was a specialist in paediatrics employed by D2 and provided medical care and treatment to P from 12 to 18 March 2014.
facts.F2: On or about 8 March 2014, P was unwell.
facts.F3: P consulted Dr Wu, a Specialist in Paediatrics, at the Out-Patient Department of D2 on 10 March 2014.
facts.F4: D1 admitted P to D2 on 12 March 2014 and ordered that P receive intravenous Claforan.
facts.F5: Between 13 and 14 March 2014, P continued to suffer from various symptoms, and D1 maintained the diagnosis of pharyngitis.
facts.F6: On 15 March 2014 at about 6:40pm, D1 examined P's abdomen and recorded that it was distended.
facts.F7: On 16 March 2014, P continued to suffer from swinging high fever, and D1 prescribed a more broad-spectrum antibiotic for treating a variety of bacterial infections.
facts.F8: On 17 March 2014 at about 6:40pm, D1 examined P and found that he had developed abdominal distensions, and an abdominal ultrasound scan to check whether P had intra-abdominal sepsis or other possible underlying conditions was arranged for the next morning.
facts.F9: At about 10:00pm, D1 was informed that P vomited greenish fluid and his blood test showed abnormal findings. D1 ordered an urgent CT scan which was done at about 11:25pm.
facts.F10: The CT scan report released at about 1:15am on 18th March 2014 revealed that gross ascites were present with associated pneumoperitoneum, intestinal obstruction was evident with generalized small bowel dilation and fluids levels, and a suspected focal mural defect was seen at the sigmoid colon which might represent the site of perforation.
facts.F11: The issue of causation in the present case requires expert evidence on the questions of (a) what action would have been undertaken had an earlier diagnosis and referral been made, (b) would that action have altered the course of the injury, and (c) if nothing different would have been done, or if the answer to (b) above is in the negative, was that below the standard of care that could be expected.
facts.F12: Prof PT was asked to give an opinion on delay in referral.

reference_issues: Whether the PT 1st/2nd Reports should be withdrawn and not adduced at the trial of the present action.

claim: claims in bailment, conversion, and negligence
requested_remedy: claims in bailment, conversion, and negligence

facts.F1: The Plaintiffs were the Consignees of electronic goods shipped from Kobe, Japan in March 1990.
facts.F2: The 4th Defendant was engaged by the 3rd Defendant to store the cargo and deliver it to the Plaintiffs.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff's goods were supposed to be packed in 96 cartons, while an additional 34 cartons were consigned to another Consignee in Hong Kong, The Hong Kong C.D. Centre.
facts.F4: The Plaintiffs discovered that 12 of the cartons had been delivered to Hong Kong C.D. Centre, resulting in a short delivery of said cartons.
facts.F5: The Plaintiffs produced evidence that they had paid for the goods they had bought.
facts.F6: Mr. Fok Ka Fai, a Transportation Clerk employed by the Plaintiffs, gave evidence that he visited the 4th Defendant's warehouse on March 20, 1990, and March 23, 1990, to collect the consignment of electronic goods.
facts.F7: Mr. Fok discovered discrepancies between the markings on the cartons and the contents of the documents, which led to the conclusion that 12 cartons had been misdelivered.
facts.F8: A Survey Report prepared by Mr. Lam, a Surveyor, confirmed that the contents of 12 cartons did not match the descriptions given in the Invoice and contained different goods to those described.
facts.F9: A statement from Mr. Chugani of Ramsons Corporation, the Consignor of the goods, described the system adopted by Ramsons when packing goods, which suggested that it was unlikely that the electronic goods would be packed in incorrect cartons.
facts.F10: Mr. Lam's Survey cost HK$500.
facts.F11: The total invoice price for the goods was Japanese Yen 937,500.
facts.F12: The 4th Defendant failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for any failure to deliver up goods to the Plaintiff as required by the terms of the Delivery Order.

reference_issues: Whether the 4th Defendant misdelivered 12 cartons of electronic goods to Hong Kong C.D. Centre.
Whether the 4th Defendant failed in its duty to deliver up all of the goods to the Plaintiff as required by the terms of the Delivery Order.

claim: The plaintiff is claiming damages for personal injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident
requested_remedy: The plaintiff is claiming damages for personal injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident

facts.F1: The accident occurred on 31st May 1970 between the plaintiff's private motor car and a public light bus owned by the 2nd defendant and driven by the 1st defendant.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was treated at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital for his injuries and was later discharged.
facts.F3: The plaintiff suffered from various injuries including multiple lacerations, keloid scarring, crepitous of the right shoulder, and a painful and tender lump on the outer aspect of the right lower arm.
facts.F4: The plaintiff's vehicle was a total write-off and he was not covered by comprehensive insurance, only third-party risk.
facts.F5: The plaintiff was employed in a rice shop at a salary of $700 per month before the accident and was unable to continue in this employment due to his injuries.
facts.F6: The plaintiff tried to find alternative employment but was unable to do so due to his lack of skills in any trade other than rice grading and sifting and his inability to do unskilled heavy labor due to his injuries.
facts.F7: The plaintiff eventually found employment at a grocery shop in a resettlement estate in June 1971 at a salary of $360 per month.
facts.F8: The court considered the evidence of three doctors, Dr. Pang Hok Tuen, Dr. Anthony Charles da Roza, and Dr. Andrew Chan, in determining the extent of the plaintiff's injuries and their impact on his ability to work.
facts.F9: The court considered the plaintiff's attempts to find alternative employment and his efforts to mitigate his damages, which took place until June 1971.
facts.F10: The court found that the plaintiff was not physically fit to resume his previous occupation, affecting his ability to work in his previous job.
facts.F11: The court considered the period of time until the plaintiff could adapt himself for some other more lucrative occupation in assessing future loss of wages.

claim: claims for damages for injuries suffered as a consequence of being knocked down by a public light bus driven by the 1st Defendant as servant and/or agent of the 2nd Defendant

facts.F1: The accident occurred on 12th March 1976 when the Plaintiff was crossing Kwun Tong Road, Kowloon from south to north and the vehicle driven by the 1st Defendant was travelling from east to west
facts.F2: The material stretch of Kwun Tong Road is divided by a railing into two parts with 3 lanes on each side for traffic travelling in opposite directions
facts.F3: The Plaintiff was crossing Kwun Tong Road on an uncontrolled stud crossing which traversed the whole of Kwun Tong Road with a gap for the crossing in the dividing railing
facts.F4: The Plaintiff was knocked down in the third lane, i.e. after he had crossed two-thirds of the westbound carriageway
facts.F5: The Plaintiff was with a group of 20 odd pedestrians waiting to cross
facts.F6: There were many vehicles on the road
facts.F7: After all vehicles had stopped the Plaintiff followed the other pedestrians to cross
facts.F8: There were 14 to 15 persons in front of him, the closest being about 2 feet in front of him, and some pedestrians followed him
facts.F9: When the Plaintiff reached the third lane he lost consciousness and did not feel the collision nor did he see the Defendant's vehicle
facts.F10: The Plaintiff recovered consciousness in hospital
facts.F11: A statement made by the Plaintiff in hospital on 7th April 1976 (26 days later) to a police officer investigating the accident stated that he was standing on the pavement ready to cross the road but that he could not remember anything after that
facts.F12: There was no mention of the vehicles being stationary nor of a group of pedestrians crossing with him in the hospital statement
facts.F13: The Plaintiff claimed to have suffered a fracture of his forehead which caused injury to his brain, but his claim of serious head injury is not supported by the medical report dated 5th November 1976 from the United Christian Hospital
facts.F14: The Plaintiff was conscious and oriented when he was admitted, that he had retrograde amnesia in that he could not remember what happened at the accident, and that there was no medical evidence of brain damage
facts.F15: The 1st Defendant was familiar with Kwun Tong Road near the vicinity of the accident
facts.F16: The 1st Defendant knew of the railing dividing the road and the existence of the stud crossing
facts.F17: The 1st Defendant was travelling in the third lane at about 28 miles per hour with a moving lorry on his left about 4 or 5 feet ahead of him when he saw the Plaintiff cross the front of the goods vehicle about 10 feet from his vehicle
facts.F18: The 1st Defendant immediately applied the emergency brake but nevertheless the left front of his vehicle knocked the Plaintiff down
facts.F19: The Plaintiff put himself in jeopardy
facts.F20: A a contributory negligence of 50% is attributed to the Plaintiff

Whether the Plaintiff was contributorily negligent

claim: Damages in the sum of $700,000
requested_remedy: Damages in the sum of $700,000
parties: Defendant: Mr. Wai and Mr. Tam Hau Ho (second defendants)

facts.F1: On 5 October 1993, the first defendant (Mr. Wai) was driving a Toyota Hi-Ace van along Cheung Sha Wan Road when the nearside rear wheel came off and struck the plaintiff.
facts.F2: A few hours before the accident, Mr. Wai had taken his van to the defendants' tyre shop.
facts.F3: Mr. Wai asked Mr. Tam Hau Ho (Mr. Tam), one of the second defendants, to exchange the wheels on the two vans.
facts.F4: Mr. Tam did the wheel exchange, but allegedly did not properly secure the nuts fastening the wheel that came off.
facts.F5: The plaintiff's damages were agreed at $700,000, and the issue was the responsibility of the defendants for the damages.
facts.F6: Mr. Wai's van was originally fitted with steel wheels, but the wheels fitted by Mr. Tam were alloy wheels with a single stud.
facts.F7: The wheels found on Mr. Wai's van after the accident were not the wheels fitted by Mr. Tam, but were alloy wheels designed to give the appearance of being fitted by a single nut.
facts.F8: Mr. Lau Kam Kong, a senior vehicle examiner, testified that the alloy wheels on Mr. Wai's van at the time of the accident were not properly secured, and that all five or possibly four of the nuts had been left loose.
facts.F9: The court received earlier statements from Mr. Tam that were found to be false and not credible by the judge
facts.F10: Mr. Wai had given earlier statements that were consistent and credible

reference_issues: Whether the second defendants were negligent in not properly securing the nuts fastening the wheel that came off.
Whether Mr. Wai was also negligent in not being aware of a problem with the van that might cause a danger to other people.

claim: damages for the death of LUK YIM PING, the deceased
requested_remedy: damages for the death of LUK YIM PING, the deceased

facts.F1: The deceased, LUK YIM PING, was 22 years old and worked as a cleaner at Man Foong Industrial Building.
facts.F2: She had given birth to a baby in China seven weeks before coming to Hong Kong and left her baby in China with her husband.
facts.F3: The deceased lived in the Western District with her father and siblings after arriving in Hong Kong.
facts.F4: She started working as a cleaner at Man Foong Industrial Building three days before the accident.
facts.F5: The deceased was allowed to collect scrap paper and discarded cardboard boxes from the industrial units in the building to sell off and pocket the proceeds herself.
facts.F6: The No. 2 lift in the building was a cargo lift that served all the floors and had been exclusively serviced and maintained by the defendant since its installation in 1977.
facts.F7: On the day of the accident, the deceased attended work as usual and had requested to use the No. 2 lift to transport rubbish/scrap paper down from the upper floors.
facts.F8: The aunt of the deceased, Law Lam Fai, found the deceased's cleaning equipment and metal rack with scrap paper unattended on the lift lobby of the 10th floor.
facts.F9: A passenger reported loud scratching noises and smoke when traveling in the No. 2 lift, and the watchman called the defendant to send someone to check the lift.
facts.F10: A lift technician from the defendant found the body of the deceased at the bottom of the lift shaft.
facts.F11: The post-mortem examination report showed that the deceased had suffered multiple fractures and brain damage, and the cause of death was put down as being caused by those multiple injuries.
facts.F12: Police investigation found no evidence of foul play or suicide.
facts.F13: The system of operation of the No. 2 lift was designed to prevent passengers from falling out of it and occupants of the building from falling into the lift shaft.
facts.F14: The deceased did not deliberately find her way into the lift shaft and her entry into the shaft was accidental.
facts.F15: The lift did not operate properly, which led to the deceased entering the lift shaft.
facts.F16: The defendant's expert, Dr. So, was unable to explain how the lift could have moved with the car door open.

Whether the defendant was negligent in maintaining the No. 2 lift

facts.F1: Multiple plaintiffs brought actions against various defendants for damages for personal injuries.
facts.F2: Prior to 2012, the courts in Hong Kong used a net rate of return of 4.5% to calculate the multiplier for future losses.
facts.F3: The Privy Council's decision in Simon v Helmot in 2012 held that the net rate of return in Guernsey was 0.5% for non-earnings-related future losses and -1.5% for earnings-related future losses.
facts.F4: Expert reports by Professor Chan Wai Sum provided evidence on the net rate of return of various investment vehicles in Hong Kong from 1995 to 2012.
facts.F5: The reports showed that the net rate of returns on most investments were substantially below 4.5% over the past decade.
facts.F6: The court followed the decision of the Court of Appeal in Chan Pui Ki v Leung On in 1996, which held that the actuarial and economic evidence adduced had failed to prove that the Cookson v Knowles assumption was wrong for Hong Kong.
facts.F7: The Ogden Tables and the Chan Tables are used in assessing multipliers for future losses.

reference_issues: Whether the assumption of a net rate of return of 4.5% remains valid in Hong Kong for calculating future losses.
Whether the Cookson v Knowles assumption should be departed from in light of the substantial change in the economic landscape since 1996.
